displayQuote: She is always kind to her inferiors. — But where does she find them?

meta.title: Who really said "She is always kind to her inferiors. — But where does she find them?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The exchange is first documented in Sidney Skolsky's 1937 Hollywood column, crediting Dorothy Parker against an unnamed actress. The famous version that names Clare Boothe Luce came later, and the dates don't fit.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'She is always kind to her inferiors. — But where does she find them?'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Dorothy Parker in a 1937 Hollywood column — aimed at an unnamed actress, not Clare Boothe Luce. The joke itself goes back to Samuel Johnson in 1770.

answer.label: Credited to Dorothy Parker — the Clare Boothe Luce version is doubted
answer.sourceLine: No primary record of this exchange survives. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest instance it could locate to Sidney Skolsky’s Hollywood column in the Milwaukee Sentinel of 23 June 1937, where the punchline is already Dorothy Parker’s and the target is only “a prominent actress.” Even that is a gossip-column report rather than a document of Parker speaking, and the joke itself is far older than she is — Boswell records a version of it from 1770.

source.heading: Where the exchange actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Milwaukee Sentinel, 23 June 1937 — the target named only as “a prominent actress”
Profiles: The Candor Kid — Part I
Boswell’s Life of Johnson (1791), on a conversation of 1770

source.excerpt: At lunch the other day, a group were discussing a prominent actress and a person said: “She’s only kind to her inferiors.” Whereupon Dorothy Parker remarked: “Where does she find them?”
trail: 1770 — Boswell records Samuel Johnson, told that a woman was remarkable for her “humility and condescension to inferiours,” observing “that those were very laudable qualities, but it might not be so easy to discover who the lady’s inferiours were” (Life of Johnson, Vol. 2 ↗, published 1791).
1882 — Mark Twain delivers Advice to Youth, inverting the same gag onto superiors: “Be respectful to your superiors, if you have any” — his only documented contact with this joke (Wikiquote ↗).

23 June 1937 — Sidney Skolsky’s Hollywood column prints the exchange with Dorothy Parker delivering the punchline and an unnamed “prominent actress” as the target — the earliest instance Quote Investigator could find (Quote Investigator ↗).

4 January 1941 — Margaret Case Harriman’s New Yorker profile of Clare Boothe Luce retells it with Luce as the target and dates the dinner to “last year” — a chronology Quote Investigator finds inconsistent with the 1937 printing (Quote Investigator ↗).

1946–1956 — The joke resurfaces on 4 April 1946 in The Castilian of Castile, New York, still credited to Parker, with the target renamed “Miss Smith”; by 21 June 1956, in The Whitewright Sun of Texas, every participant is anonymous (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Sidney Skolsky’s Hollywood column in the Milwaukee Sentinel, 23 June 1937 — the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗. Note that no name is given for the actress, and that the wording is “only kind,” not the smoother “always kind” of the version that circulates today.

source.rightsHolder: The New Yorker (Margaret Case Harriman’s 1941 profile) and the Milwaukee Sentinel (Sidney Skolsky’s 1937 column)
source.rightsNote: The 18th-century ancestor is safely public domain — Boswell’s Life of Johnson was published in 1791. The exchange in its modern form, however, is documented only in 20th-century periodicals: Skolsky’s column of 1937 and Harriman’s New Yorker profile of 1941, both well after 1931, so those texts are treated as in-copyright to their publishers. Because no primary record of Parker speaking the line exists, no earlier public-domain source can be claimed for it.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: About Dorothy Parker
author.bio: Dorothy Parker made her name as a theatre critic for Vanity Fair and then as a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, the New York circle whose remarks were recycled daily in newspaper columns. She wrote drama reviews and verse for The New Yorker from its founding in 1925, and later worked in Hollywood, earning Academy Award nominations for A Star Is Born (1937) and Smash-Up, the Story of a Woman (1947). Her reputation for the perfect one-line demolition is exactly why lines like this one accumulate around her — and why a columnist’s single sentence became the whole provenance.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: Quote Investigator opens its study of this exchange with a row of candidate names: Dorothy Parker, Mark Twain, Samuel Johnson, Sidney Skolsky, Margaret Case Harriman, Anonymous — a list that mixes possible speakers, older precursors and the two journalists who printed the item. Only Dorothy Parker has a dated citation as the speaker of this exchange.

items.scope: The name it gets confused with
items.why: No instance of this exchange appears in Twain’s work, and Quote Investigator ↗ locates no Twain citation for it — it lists him for a variant, not for this dialogue. What Twain actually wrote is the mirror-image joke — “Be respectful to your superiors, if you have any” — in his 1882 talk Advice to Youth, which questions the existence of superiors, not inferiors (Wikiquote ↗).

The version everyone repeats names Luce, and comes from Margaret Case Harriman’s New Yorker profile of 4 January 1941, which places the dinner “last year.” But the punchline was already in print as Parker’s in June 1937, and the 1937 item calls the target “a prominent actress” — a description that fits the actress Claire Luce far better than the playwright of The Women (Quote Investigator ↗).

Boswell records Johnson, asked to write a funeral sermon and told the deceased was remarkable for her “humility and condescension to inferiours,” replying that those were laudable qualities but that it might not be easy to discover who the lady’s inferiours were (Life of Johnson, Vol. 2 ↗). In the 1700s “condescension” meant courtesy across ranks, not contempt.

misattribution.truthLine: As far as the printed record goes, the exchange belongs to Dorothy Parker — first documented in Sidney Skolsky’s column of 23 June 1937, with an unnamed actress as the target — and the joke itself is older than Twain, Parker and the movies alike (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why this joke keeps finding new owners
lead: The gag is a trapdoor. Someone offers a compliment built on social hierarchy — she is gracious to those beneath her — and the reply simply asks who those people are supposed to be. The praise collapses into an insult without a single rude word being spoken, which is why the same three seconds of dialogue have been re-cast with a new victim roughly once a generation.

That reusability is also why the attribution drifts. A joke with no fixed target and no fixed speaker attaches itself to whoever the era considers its sharpest tongue: Samuel Johnson in the 18th century, Dorothy Parker in the 20th, and Mark Twain whenever the internet needs a name that guarantees a share.
detailsBody: The version everyone repeats names Clare Boothe Luce as the target, and it comes from Margaret Case Harriman’s New Yorker profile of Luce published 4 January 1941, which sets the scene at a Hollywood dinner “last year.”

Quote Investigator points out the chronology does not work: the punchline had already been printed as Parker’s in June 1937. It also notes that Skolsky’s 1937 item described the target as a “prominent actress,” which does not fit Luce — whose fame rested on writing the 1936 Broadway hit The Women — but would fit the separate, genuinely well-known actress Claire Luce.
context.pull: The punchline survives every rewrite. Only the speaker’s name changes.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest instance of the exchange located by QI is Sidney Skolsky's Hollywood column, Milwaukee Sentinel, 23 June 1937, crediting Dorothy Parker with 'Where does she find them?' against an unnamed 'prominent actress'; the Clare Boothe Luce version comes from Margaret Case Harriman's New Yorker profile of 4 January 1941, whose 'last year' chronology QI finds inconsistent; precursors include Samuel Johnson (1770, via Boswell), Elsie Dinsmore (1867), Mark Twain's Advice to Youth (1882) and Smart Set fillers (1903, 1916); QI lists Mark Twain among the names the quip is credited to.

Boswell's Life of Johnson, Volume 2, in the 1770 section, contains: 'being told she was remarkable for her humility and condescension to inferiours, he observed, that those were very laudable qualities, but it might not be so easy to discover who the lady's inferiours were.'
Project Gutenberg ebook 9072 is 'Life of Johnson, Volume 2' by James Boswell, a biography published in 1791.

Wikiquote's Mark Twain page carries 'Be respectful to your superiors, if you have any.' sourced to the speech 'Advice to Youth', Saturday Morning Club, Boston, 15 April 1882, in the general sourced Quotes section — and does NOT contain the 'kind to her inferiors' / 'where does she find them' exchange.
Wikiquote's Dorothy Parker page does not contain the 'kind to her inferiors' / 'where does she find them' exchange in any section, and gives her dates as 22 August 1893 – 7 June 1967.

Dorothy Parker (August 22, 1893 – June 7, 1967) was an American poet, literary critic and writer of fiction; founding member of the Algonquin Round Table; theatre critic for Vanity Fair from 1918; contributor to The New Yorker from its 1925 founding; Academy Award nominations for A Star Is Born (1937) and Smash-Up, the Story of a Woman (1947).

The full text of Mark Twain's 'Advice to Youth' contains 'Be respectful to your superiors, if you have any, also to strangers, and sometimes to others.'; the page dates the talk to 15 April 1882 at the Saturday Morning Club, Boston.
Clare Boothe Luce (March 10, 1903 – October 9, 1987) wrote the Broadway play 'The Women', which opened in 1936, and was a magazine editor, congresswoman and ambassador — not an actress.
Claire Luce (1903–1989) was a separate American stage and screen actress active in the 1930s, and Wikipedia carries a hatnote distinguishing her from Clare Boothe Luce.
Wikipedia's 'Advice to Youth' article dates the essay to 1882 and notes the audience is uncertain, with editor's notes conjecturally assigning the address to the Boston Saturday Morning Club.
